narrative:
Your law school application was denied because the model estimated a 56.8% probability that you would fail the bar exam on the first attempt. In practical terms, that is a slightly greater chance of failing than passing, so the admissions decision treated you as a higher-risk applicant rather than a clear likely passer.

The strongest factor was your third-year class rank: you were in the second decile, while accepted students averaged around the sixth decile. That gap strongly pushed the prediction toward bar failure. The second-most important factor was your undergraduate GPA. At 3.20, it is only slightly below the accepted-student average of 3.23, and it actually worked in your favor, pushing the prediction toward passing and acting as a relative strength. The third-most important factor was your first-year class rank. You were also in the second decile there, compared with an accepted-student average near the sixth decile, and this pushed toward failure, though less strongly than your third-year rank.

To improve a future application, focus on showing stronger and sustained academic performance, especially in upper-year law coursework, and address the bar-exam risk directly through study skills, academic advising, and bar preparation planning. You should also consider retaking the LSAT or strengthening other admissions evidence, then reapply once you can show a clearer upward trajectory.
